description: Discovery batch for new Brali Protocol candidates mapped to existing Growth Zones. These records expand the research queue only: they do not promote a public hack to reviewed status. Promotion still requires a separate Evidence Decision and protocol implementation under SOURCE_POLICY.md.

research_candidates.title: Prequestioning and Pretesting Effects: a Review of Empirical Research, Theoretical Perspectives, and Implications for Educational Practice
research_candidates.review_notes: High-priority new-protocol lead. The full open-access review was inspected. A useful Brali action would ask the learner a small set of concrete questions before reading, watching or listening, allow an honest guess, then require an immediate opportunity to find and correct the answer. The evidence is strongest for information directly targeted by the prequestions; benefits for untested material and complex transfer are less reliable. Wrong initial answers are expected rather than treated as failure. Do not turn this into a claim that guessing broadly improves intelligence, comprehension or transfer, and do not invent an optimal question count or timing rule.

research_candidates.title: Effect of exercise snacks on fitness and cardiometabolic health in physically inactive individuals: systematic review and meta-analysis
research_candidates.review_notes: Strong 2026 discovery lead for a time-friction protocol: replace the all-or-nothing idea of a workout with brief structured bouts distributed through the day. The meta-analysis included 11 RCTs (n=414) and defined exercise snacks as bouts of five minutes or less performed at least twice daily, at least three days per week, for at least two weeks. Moderate-certainty evidence supported improved cardiorespiratory fitness in physically inactive adults; evidence for muscular endurance in older adults was very low certainty, and the review did not support claims about body composition, blood pressure or lipid improvement. A future public protocol must not present exercise snacks as a substitute for all physical-activity guidance or prescribe near-maximal intensity without an explicit safety boundary. Full source review is still required before an Evidence Decision.

research_candidates.title: After Dinner Rest a While, After Supper Walk a Mile? A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis on the Acute Postprandial Glycemic Response to Exercise Before and After Meal Ingestion in Healthy Subjects and Patients with Impaired Glucose Tolerance
research_candidates.review_notes: High-priority bounded health-behavior lead. The full open-access systematic review and meta-analysis was inspected. Across eight randomized crossover trials (116 participants), post-meal exercise reduced acute postprandial glucose excursions compared with inactive control and, overall, compared with pre-meal exercise; earlier post-meal activity appeared more favorable than longer delays. Walking was a common intervention, but protocols varied substantially in duration, intensity, meal composition and population. All included trials had high overall risk of bias and the evidence base was small. A Brali protocol should therefore say 'put comfortable movement close to a meal when practical' rather than promise disease prevention, prescribe one universal walking duration, or make medication/diabetes-management claims.
